legal.headline: Delhi HC quashes ED LOCs against non- accused in RCFLRHFL case; Holds mere pendency of investigation insufficient to restrict travel
legal.hook: While upholding its writ jurisdiction against an alternative remedy, it directed that the petitioners’ availability be secured through cooperation and travel-intimation conditions instead
legal.summary: While upholding its writ jurisdiction against an alternative remedy, it directed that the petitioners’ availability be secured through cooperation and travel-intimation conditions instead Delhi High Court: While quashing Look Out Circulars (LOCs) opened by Enforcement Directorate (ED) against the non- accused petitioners, a Single Judge Bench of Madhu Jain, J., held that the pendency of an investigation does not, by itself, justify restricting a person’s right to travel abroad, which forms part of personal liberty under Article 21 of the Constitution of India . While upholding its jurisdiction under Article 226, it held that an alternative remedy ordinarily warrants restraint but does not oust its writ jurisdiction.
legal.contextNote: The Delhi High Court (Single Judge Bench, Madhu Jain, J.) quashed Enforcement Directorate (ED) Look‑Out Circulars (LOCs) issued against petitioners who were not named as accused in the RCFL‑RHFL matter. The bench held that mere pendency of an ED investigation does not, per se, justify curtailing international travel, invoking Article 21 (right to personal liberty) and affirming its writ jurisdiction under Article 226. The court ordered that the petitioners’ availability be secured via cooperation and travel‑intimation conditions rather than blanket travel bans. No specific statutory provision was cited; the decision rests on constitutional principles and the High Court’s inherent power to grant relief against arbitrary executive action.
